Most introductory statistics quietly assumes observations can be treated as independent.

Time series often refuses to cooperate.

Yesterday can predict today. December can resemble last December. A trend can make the future unlike the past average.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn
- Trend, seasonality, noise and autocorrelation
- Lagged relationships
- Why random train/test splitting can leak the future
- Rolling-origin backtesting
- How statistical forecasting connects to ML
:::

## A time-series decomposition

A useful conceptual model is

$$
Y_t=T_t+S_t+R_t,
$$

where:

- $T_t$ = trend,
- $S_t$ = seasonal component,
- $R_t$ = remainder/noise.

## Interactive: build a signal

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof trendTS = Inputs.range([0,.08], {value:.02, step:.005, label:"Trend per step"})
viewof ampTS = Inputs.range([0,5], {value:2, step:.1, label:"Seasonal amplitude"})
viewof noiseTS = Inputs.range([0,4], {value:1, step:.1, label:"Noise"})
rts=d3.randomLcg(.64)
seriesTS=d3.range(180).map(t=>({t,y:10+trendTS*t+ampTS*Math.sin(2*Math.PI*t/30)+(rts()-.5)*2*noiseTS}))
Plot.plot({
 height:330,x:{label:"Time"},y:{label:"y"},
 marks:[Plot.line(seriesTS,{x:"t",y:"y",stroke:"#4F46E5",strokeWidth:2})]
})
```

Change one component at a time. The observed line is the mixture.

## Autocorrelation

Autocorrelation at lag $k$ compares $Y_t$ with $Y_{t-k}$.

A strong lag-7 relationship in daily data may indicate weekly seasonality.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go

rng=np.random.default_rng(18)
t=np.arange(365)
y=20+.02*t+3*np.sin(2*np.pi*t/7)+rng.normal(0,1.2,len(t))

lags=np.arange(1,31)
acf=[np.corrcoef(y[k:],y[:-k])[0,1] for k in lags]

fig=go.Figure(go.Bar(x=lags,y=acf))
fig.update_layout(height=340,xaxis_title="Lag",yaxis_title="Autocorrelation")
fig.show()
```

## The cardinal rule: do not train on the future

Random splitting can create leakage:

```text
BAD FOR MANY TIME-SERIES TASKS
past + future mixed → random train/test
```

Prefer chronological evaluation:

```text
TRAIN                 TEST
───────────────|────────────
past                     future
```

## Animation: rolling-origin backtesting

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px

rng=np.random.default_rng(19)
t=np.arange(160)
y=10+.04*t+2*np.sin(2*np.pi*t/20)+rng.normal(0,.7,len(t))
rows=[]
for cutoff in [60,80,100,120,140]:
    for i,(tt,yy) in enumerate(zip(t,y)):
        part="train" if tt<=cutoff else "future"
        rows.append({"cutoff":cutoff,"time":tt,"y":yy,"part":part})
df=pd.DataFrame(rows)
fig=px.scatter(df,x="time",y="y",color="part",animation_frame="cutoff",
               range_x=[0,160],range_y=[5,20])
fig.update_layout(height=380)
fig.show()
```

Each frame moves the training frontier forward. This is much closer to how forecasting models are used in reality.

## DS/ML Bridge

Statistical forecasting and ML share the same core evaluation discipline:

```text
features from past only
      ↓
fit model
      ↓
predict unseen future
      ↓
advance time
      ↓
repeat
```

ML models may use lag features, rolling statistics, calendar features and exogenous variables. Statistical models may encode trend, autoregression and seasonality directly.

The algorithm matters—but **temporal validation design matters first**.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Leakage can make a bad forecast look excellent
Any feature computed using information unavailable at prediction time can invalidate evaluation, even if the code runs perfectly.
:::

## What should you save?

```text
forecast_run/
├── data_cutoff.txt
├── feature_config.json
├── split_definition.json
├── model_config.json
├── forecasts.csv
└── metrics.json
```

A forecast is inseparable from the time at which it was made.

## Summary
- Time series contain ordered dependence.
- Trend, seasonality and autocorrelation create structure across time.
- Random splitting can leak future information.
- Rolling-origin evaluation mimics real forecasting.
- Statistical and ML forecasting differ in machinery but share the need for leakage-safe temporal validation.
